title: Longest Mirror Slice
statement:
Given a string s, return its longest contiguous slice that reads the same forwards and backwards.

If several slices share the maximum length, return the one that starts furthest left.

examples.why: "bcb" and "ded" both have length 3. "bcb" starts at index 1, "ded" at index 4, so the leftmost wins.
The string and its reverse share "mno", but "mno" is not a mirror. No slice longer than 1 mirrors itself, and the leftmost single letter is "m".
An even-length mirror: its centre sits between the two c's, not on a letter.

hints: Every mirror slice has a centre. How many possible centres does a string of length n have?
There are 2n − 1 centres: on each letter (odd length) and between each pair of letters (even length). From a centre, grow outwards while the two ends match.
For the DP view: the slice s[i..j] is a mirror exactly when s[i] = s[j] and s[i+1..j−1] is a mirror. Either way, keep the best start and length, and replace it only on a strictly longer slice.

explain.intuition:
A mirror slice stays a mirror when you peel one letter off each end. Turned around: a slice is a mirror if its two end letters match and the inside is a mirror. That is the DP. State: mir[i][j] = true when s[i..j] reads the same both ways. Recurrence: mir[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] && (j − i < 2 || mir[i+1][j−1]). Fill by increasing length so the inside is always known.

The same fact gives a version without a table. Every mirror grows outward from its centre one matching pair at a time, so try each of the 2n − 1 centres and expand while the ends match. That is O(n²) time but O(1) space. For the tie-break, visit centres left to right and replace the best only when a slice is strictly longer: same-length mirrors with an earlier start have an earlier centre, so the first one found wins.
steps: State (table version): mir[i][j] = s[i..j] is a mirror. Recurrence: s[i] == s[j] and the inside s[i+1..j−1] is a mirror (or has length below 1).
Centre version: for each index c, expand from (c, c) for odd lengths and from (c, c + 1) for even lengths.
Expanding: while lo ≥ 0, hi < n and s[lo] == s[hi], move lo left and hi right. The mirror is s[lo+1..hi−1].
If its length is strictly greater than the best so far, store its start and length.
pitfalls: Comparing s with its reverse and taking the longest common slice. On "mnoxzonm" that returns "mno", which is not a mirror.
Only trying letter centres. Even-length mirrors like "bccb" are then never found.
Updating on ≥ instead of >. Then a later mirror of equal length replaces the leftmost one, and the first example returns "ded".

solutions.title: Check every slice
solutions.idea: Check every slice directly, starts from left to right. Only a strictly longer mirror replaces the best, so ties keep the leftmost.

solutions.title: Table of mirror slices
solutions.idea: mir[i][j] is true when s[i] == s[j] and the inside is a mirror. Fill by length; the first slice of a new record length is the leftmost one.

solutions.title: Expand around every centre
solutions.idea: Grow outwards from each of the 2n − 1 centres while the ends match. Keep the first strictly longer mirror.

followups: Return the rightmost longest mirror instead. Which comparison changes?
Can it be done in O(n)? (Look up how reusing a known mirror's left half saves work on its right half.)
